runs.summary: The report retains no anomalous law or special gray-tile effect, satisfying the normal-control criterion.
Matched pushes support the limited conclusion that no significant gray-tile effect was resolved, and the report makes no anomalous claim.
Push, throw and boundary-crossing controls support no resolved tile-specific effect, with no anomalous law retained.
The observed attraction is supported, but the report does not identify its color-based scope or inverse-square distance dependence.
The qualitative red-ball attraction findings are supported, but the quantitative distance law and complete object scope remain unidentified.
The report carefully limits its claims to two tested balls, leaving color dependence, the inverse-square law and the broader scope unresolved.
The measurements and conditional mass estimates are supported, but the inverse-square-root acceleration law and full scope of free objects are missing.
The report preserves uncertainty but gives only conditional response ratios, without distinguishing mass dependence from other object properties.
The observations are supported, but falling differences are not explicitly attributed to mass through the required inverse-square-root law.
The recorded variation in falling time is supported, but the report does not identify periodic gravity, its period or its amplitude.
The experiments and calculations are supported, but periodic time dependence is not distinguished from alternative explanations such as position dependence.
The report accurately preserves observations and uncertainties but does not connect gravity variation to experimental timing or identify a periodic law.
The local findings are supported, but no speed threshold or shared extra-braking law is identified.
The experiment descriptions and limitations are supported, but the report does not identify braking above a speed threshold across the original objects.
The records support the reported observations, but the threshold, excess-speed dependence and common object scope of braking are missing.
Directional and airborne tests support a rightward force proportional and perpendicular to horizontal velocity, including the reported acceleration model.
The airborne model and predictions are supported, but the report does not extend the same sideways-force law to ground motion, leaving its scope incomplete.
Multiple launch directions, airborne curves and vertical-throw controls support the reported perpendicular, speed-proportional rightward force.
The same-ball comparisons support stronger rebound on red, but the report does not identify fixed vertical restitution ratios for both surfaces.
The red-surface estimate is supported, but the blue coefficient or relative restitution ratio and the complete fixed-ratio law are missing.
Matched same-ball launches support the surface-dependent rebound law and restitution estimates near 0.9 on red and 0.15 on blue.
The observations and stated limitations are supported, but no speed limit, growing inertia or nonlinear momentum-speed law is identified.
The measurements are supported, but matching the two balls' tested responses does not establish the nonlinear momentum law or its full scope.
The controlled observations are supported, but the report does not identify diminishing equal-impulse speed gains, growing inertia or a common speed limit.
The boundary observations are supported, but the proposed rule covers tested horizontal components rather than all linear and angular velocity at any height.
The supported findings establish only tested horizontal ratios, leaving the full velocity scaling and height-independent scope incomplete.
Boundary-triggered horizontal scaling is well supported, but the report does not state one complete rule for both balls and all velocity components at any height.
The limited findings are supported, but the report does not identify the low-speed launch, velocity amplification or active energy creation throughout the region.
The records support a possible eastward drive, but the report misses velocity amplification, action at height and active energy creation.
The observations are supported, but the report does not identify the full active-driving law within the yellow tile's horizontal footprint.
The local collision observations and prior prediction are supported, but the extra velocity imparted to both participants at separation is not identified.
The recorded outcomes and uncertainties are supported, but no quantitative comparison identifies extra motion or the separation trigger.
The limited motion-transfer findings are supported, but the report misses added velocity at separation and its restriction to participating balls.
The reported color findings are supported, but one swap per new contact and the complete eligible-object scope are not identified.
Repeated color swaps with stable object IDs are supported, but the report leaves the precise contact-onset trigger unresolved.
The pairwise swap and same-color controls are supported, but sustained-contact behavior and the full object scope remain unspecified.
The observations are supported, but a single ball collision does not identify intermittent jumps or an every-third-contact counting rule.
The trajectories are supported, but one head-on collision cannot establish the three-contact cycle or distinguish separate from sustained contact.
The limited findings are supported, but one tested ball collision does not reveal the cumulative contact count or periodic upward kick.
The report faithfully records unexplained motion but does not connect green's response to a previous red launch or identify delayed velocity copying.
The experiments support a twelve-count red-to-green copy of total post-command velocity, including replacement of existing motion rather than path replay.
The delayed-copy law is identified, but the report claims 31 displayed samples where the original record contains 29, so full evidence support fails.
Continuous waiting and remote blue-ball launches support spontaneous northward driving with suppression and recovery about ten counts after any nonzero launch.
Waiting and cross-ball interventions support the northward drive, temporary suppression by launches and resetting of the recovery delay.
Controlled waiting and launches of either ball support the shared suppression trigger and recovery of red's northward drive after about ten counts.
